## Introduction

This traces one institutional function — the stewardship of research data at UCLA — across six
decades and five different institutional homes. It is not a straight line. The unit's name,
organizational home, and formal scope changed repeatedly; what stayed constant was a
responsibility to make research evidence findable, usable, and preserved, extended again and
again to new kinds of evidence as the objects of research changed. A 1961 archive of punch-card
survey data and a 2024 platform processing petabytes of restricted voter records are
recognizably continuous work — the same responsibility carried to new kinds of evidence — but
the scale, the methods, and the institutional stakes changed enormously along the way, and this
account tries not to read today's vocabulary backward onto earlier decades.

A full evidentiary companion — complete people roster, project inventories, visualization
methodology, and open discrepancies not yet resolved — is at
[history-companion.qmd](history-companion.html); this document is the narrative, not the full record.

## The history in 30 seconds

- UCLA's data archive traces to **1961**, when political scientist Dwaine Marvick founded the
  **Political Behavior Archive**.
- It moved through several institutional homes over six decades — never a single continuous
  organization, but a continuous *function*, re-housed as the campus around it changed: a survey
  center (1964), a research institute (1974), a formally-named archive within that institute
  (1977), the same institute renamed (~2009) and then gone (~2011), and finally its own unit
  inside the UCLA Library (2014).
- Two long-running recurring survey series — **LAMAS** (1970-1976) and its successor **LACSS**
  (1992-2002+) — are the closest thing to a continuous data product across that span, with
  **SCSS** bridging the gap between them.
- One person, **Elizabeth "Libbie" Stephenson**, is documented staffing or directing the archive
  from the late 1970s (ICPSR's own retirement profile dates her UCLA start to ~1977; other
  sources document her from 1986) to her retirement in **2016** — the clearest human through-line
  across the institutional changes.
- In **2018**, the archive's umbrella became the **Data Science Center**, which extended the same
  stewardship mission to new kinds of research data — 3D and spatial capture, restricted/sensitive
  datasets, and curriculum itself as a citable output.

## A note on the author's position

Tim Dennis directed the Social Science Data Archive and the Data Science Center from April 2017
through 2026. This is his account of the archive's history, written to leave a durable record of
a function that ran continuously for six decades and is now being reorganized out of its
standalone form. It is a perspective, not a neutral chronicle — no institutional history is. But
the record it rests on is held to a plain standard:

- Contemporary claims are tied to cited institutional records, not to memory. Because the author
  took part in the recent decades, those are held to a higher documentation standard than the
  earlier ones, not a looser one.
- Evaluative judgments — what worked, what mattered, what was lost — are marked as judgments.
- Causal claims don't outrun the evidence.
- Work done by a team is credited to the team; individual attribution only where authorship,
  formal authority, or accountability is historically material.

Evidence cutoff: **2026-08-31**. Corrections and version history are in the project repository.
Fuller detail on sources and their limits is in
[Methods and limitations](#methods-and-limitations).

## 1961-1964: The Political Behavior Archive

Political scientist Dwaine Marvick, who had joined UCLA's faculty in 1954, founded the
**Political Behavior Archive (PBA)** in 1961 [@marvickInMemoriam]. Rice and Southall situate it
in the field's founding cohort: UCLA's data service ranks as the fourth-oldest social-science
data library in their sample, after the Roper Center (1957), Berkeley (1958), and GESIS (1960),
and ahead of ICPSR itself (1962) [@riceSouthall2016]. The PBA's stewardship object was
straightforward for its moment: distributing survey and behavioral data from ICPR, the Roper
Public Opinion Research Center, and local holdings to UCLA researchers [@stilesStephenson2008].
Marvick was, per a UC memorial, "an early advocate and practitioner of computer applications to
political data" — which makes founding an archive a well-contextualized move for him, though no
source found so far states his own reason for doing it in 1961 specifically. That gap is
notable: Heinz Eulau's detailed 1999 memorial covers Marvick's career at length and never
mentions the archive at all.[^eulau]

The following year, **UCLA was among the founding member institutions of ICPSR**. This is
confirmed against the primary document — Warren Miller's August 1962 memo to Rensis Likert
making the case for the consortium names the members "as of July 30, 1962," and "University of
California at Los Angeles" is on the list.[^miller-memo] Two things often attached to that fact
are shakier, and both trace to the same place: the text Libbie Stephenson wrote for the
archive's Dataverse page, which says there were **eight** founding members and that UCLA joined
"through [Marvick's] efforts." That is the archive's institutional memory, not an independent
record. A longtime ICPSR staff member's membership-records list has **22** original institutions
(Miller's memo lists 21), and the "8" may instead refer to a "Committee of Eight" whose 1962–63
correspondence sits in ICPSR's own archive — a founding committee, not the dues-paying roster. And no document found so far,
Miller's memo included, gives Marvick a formal role in the 1962 founding; his documented ICPSR
involvement is governing-board service from **1964**, rising to chair of the ICPR Council in
**1966–67**. What *is* documented is that Marvick and Miller were close friends and
collaborators from the early 1950s at Michigan's Survey Research Center — a plausible channel
for "through his efforts," but not proof of it.[^eulau]

[^miller-memo]: Warren E. Miller, memo to Rensis Likert, August 1962 (`evidence/miller-1962-considerations.md`)
— the actual founding document, not a later description of it. Cross-checked against Erik
Austin's ICPSR founding-members list (`evidence/icpsr-founding-members-austin.md`). The "8
members" / "through his efforts" phrasing is from `evidence/ssda-harvard-dataverse-about.md`
(written by Stephenson).

[^eulau]: Heinz Eulau, "Good-bye to Two Dear Friends: Warren Miller and Dwaine Marvick — A
Personal Memoir," 1999 (`evidence/eulau-1999-miller-marvick-memoir.md`).

## 1964-1974: The Survey Research Center years

The archive's next home was UCLA's **Survey Research Center (SRC)**, formed in 1964, which
housed an **"Archival Data Library"** into which the PBA merged [@stilesStephenson2008].
Marvick's own August 1964 proposal — *"Plans for the Development of a Social Science Archival
Data Library in the UCLA Survey Research Center"* [@marvick1967proposal] — set out the concept
directly, though the document itself hasn't been located yet (see
[history-companion.qmd](history-companion.html)).

This is the point worth being precise about, because the archive's *founding date* is told
several ways and the confusion is avoidable. The archive *function* — accessioning the datasets
of the tape-sharing and mainframe era, keeping their codebooks, documenting them, and running a
reference room where researchers could work out how to use machine-readable data — was a formal
part of the SRC from 1964, and of the PBA before it. What it was not yet was a *named unit* with
its own staff line or consultative services: per Stiles and Stephenson, the SRC's Archival Data
Library operated "on a reference-room basis only." The name and the formal unit come in 1977;
the work is older.

(One internal detail remains unresolved: the archive's own account — the text Libbie Stephenson
wrote for its Dataverse page — places the 1964 SRC arrangement "under the direction of Eve
Fielder," but a published obituary says Fielder became SRC's first director only in 1976. Either
SRC ran from 1964 under someone else, or the account compresses two events — see
[history-companion.qmd](history-companion.html).[^fielder])

The SRC's stewardship object during this decade was the **Los Angeles Metropolitan Area Surveys
(LAMAS)**: ten waves, 1970-1976, a shared omnibus survey repeated roughly twice yearly with
rotating researcher-submitted questions [@stilesStephenson2008; @pawlockiStephenson1988].

The decade's clearest external consequence came from outside the archive itself: around 1970,
UCLA Library's Public Affairs Service, under Mary Ryan, purchased 1970 census tapes from
DUALabs — the library's first foray into numeric data, and one cited nationally as an
early/paradigm case for library involvement in machine-readable data [@roweRyan1974; @dodd1982].

[^fielder]: The "1964, under Eve Fielder" claim originates in the archive's own Dataverse-page
text (`evidence/ssda-harvard-dataverse-about.md`, written by Stephenson) and is repeated in the
2017 internal decks. The conflicting obituary date is in the 7-31 research pass
(`evidence/deep-research-report.md`). Not yet resolved against SRC's own records or the relevant
UCLA General Catalog.

## 1974-1977: ISSR, and the archive gets a name

The **Institute for Social Science Research (ISSR)** was established in 1974, incorporating the
SRC and its archival data library, under founding director **Howard E. Freeman**, a medical
sociologist [@stilesStephenson2008]. Three years later, then-Associate Director **Donald
Treiman** did what several sources describe in different words: he took the archival data
library that had run "on a reference-room basis only" and **designed its research-support
framework** — the partnership-across-the-research-lifecycle model the archive still describes as
its mission — formalizing it into a named service unit, the **Social Science Data Archive
(SSDA)**, with its own Data Archivist line [@stilesStephenson2008; @pawlockiStephenson1988]. An
OECD international directory dates the "ISSR Data Archive at UCLA" to **December 1977**, for
quantitative research "primarily secondary analysis."[^issr-1977]

So "1977" is not the archive's founding — the archive dates itself to 1961, and the function ran
continuously through the PBA and the SRC's Archive Data Library. 1977 is when it was named,
given a staff line, and built out from a reference room into a consultative service. The sources
that seem to disagree are mostly describing different facets of that one event: the archive's
own account (Stephenson) credits **Treiman** with the framework and doesn't mention ISSR; the
2017 decks and the OECD directory name **ISSR** as the home; the team's published book chapter
[@dennisEtal2021] says "as part of the **Survey Research Center**," which by 1977 was a component
of ISSR. What still needs a documentary check is the precise reporting line — whether Treiman's
1977 framework sat directly under ISSR or under SRC-within-ISSR — not the year or the continuity.
(1974 and 1977 are, in any case, separate events, not one date told two ways.)

The consequence worth noting here runs against the direction most of this history moves in:
around 1980, when UCLA Library declined to purchase 1980 census tapes, ISSR/SSDA took them on
instead, along with all associated support and storage — numeric-data stewardship moved from the
Library to the Archive [@stilesStephenson2008], the reverse of the direction it would move in
2014.

[^issr-1977]: OECD international directory of social science data archives, cited in
`evidence/deep-research-report.md`; the four-way framing conflict and the catalog evidence are
in the same pass and `site/issr-era.qmd`.

## 1977-2014: SSDA under ISSR, then ISR, then on its own

The archive's 37 years under this umbrella were not one continuous arrangement. They break into
three subperiods:[^three-subperiods]

- **ISSR proper (1977 – late 2000s).** The archive as a service unit of the Institute for Social
  Science Research. Directors identified for ISSR across this span: **Howard E. Freeman**
  (founding, into roughly 1980), **Marilynn B. Brewer** (documented in 1983), and **David O.
  Sears** (1993–2008, per his own CV).
- **Institute for Social Research (~2009–2011).** By the 2009–10 UCLA General Catalog the parent
  institute had been renamed ISR — same phone number, same components including the Data
  Archive, a new website. No director has been identified under this name.
- **Standalone SSDA (~2011–2014).** By the 2011–12 catalog neither ISSR nor ISR appears; the
  Social Science Data Archive is listed independently as a Social Sciences collection with its
  own site. No public source names a formal dissolution of the parent institute or a single
  successor. The exact reporting line from here to the 2014 Library transfer is unresolved.

SSDA's recurring survey work continued under the LAMAS model throughout, renamed and reshaped:
the **Southern California Social Survey (SCSS)**, then the **Los Angeles County Social Survey
(LACSS)**, confirmed running through 1992-2002 (see [history-companion.qmd](history-companion.html)
for the full series detail). By the 1990s the archive had become, in its own staff's words, "the
de facto campus-wide data service unit," serving public health, education, policy studies, law,
and management, not just social science departments [@stilesStephenson2008]. Early staff visible
in a surviving ~1979 SSDA newsletter include **Martin Pawlocki** (programmer), **Gina Jamison** —
the same person as today's DSC staff member Jina "Jamie" Jamison — and **Shirley Lane**, who came
from the UCLA Research Library's machine-readable 1970 Census project; the newsletter places the
archive in the Gayley Center Building by 1979, after an earlier stint in Franz Hall.[^newsletter]

The clearest human through-line for the whole era is **Elizabeth "Libbie" Stephenson**. ICPSR's
own retirement profile puts her UCLA start around **1977** — the year the archive became a named
ISSR unit — and she is documented as staff and later Director through the 2014 transfer,
retiring in **2016** [@pawlockiStephenson1988; @stephenson2013dodd; @dotyEtal2014].[^stephenson]
Read in hindsight, her career-long work on bibliographic control (with Sue Dodd's scholarship,
IASSIST, and ICPSR) is early data-citation practice, in the vocabulary a much later era would use
for the same underlying task: making data properly identified and findable. By 2013, immediately
before the Library transfer, SSDA was experimenting with the DDI-Lifecycle metadata standard and
Colectica curation software — the archive was already moving toward modern research-data
practice on its own. The era's clearest external consequence was cross-national: the
Intergenerational Stratification and Mobility File (ISMF), built with Harry Ganzeboom (Free
University, Amsterdam) and Donald Treiman, funded by the Netherlands Organisation for Scientific
Research [@stilesStephenson2008].

[^three-subperiods]: The three-subperiod structure and the director list come from the 7-31

Michael Greenwell, Madeleine De Maria, Tana Wong, among others — see
[history-companion.qmd](history-companion.html).

[^newsletter]: `evidence/newsletter-images-2017-deck.md` — photographed excerpts of a ~1979 SSDA

## 2014-2018: The Library MOU, and a change of director

The 2014 (effective)/2015 (executed) MOU transferred SSDA from the Social Sciences Division to
the UCLA Library — the first time the archive exited ISSR to become a standalone unit. It
carried 2.0 FTE, ~$245K in permanent funds, and ~$29K in subscriptions (ICPSR, Roper, UC
Berkeley/SDA, Colectica/Algenta), plus a small foundation gift fund; staff continuity included
Elizabeth Stephenson and Jina "Jamie" Jamison [@uclaSsdaMou2014]. The MOU's stated purpose was
to *expand access to the archive's expertise while modernizing its services* — a mandate to
grow the function, not just relocate it. It also carried a consultation clause: if the Library
later made "substantial changes to the operations of Social Sciences Data Archives," it was to
meet with the Social Sciences Division and ensure continuity of faculty access.

**In April 2017, Tim Dennis was hired as Director of SSDA, succeeding Stephenson**, whose own
tenure reached back to the late 1970s.[^tim-hire] That November, Dennis presented "Library Data
Archive" to UCLA Library staff, already framing 1961-2017 as one continuous arc under the
tagline "Providing archive and data services since 1961" [@dennis2017deck].

The team then ran a **design-thinking redesign** of the unit's goals and services, centering
"the user as the scholar in need of research support" [@dennisEtal2021]. In **Spring 2018** the
result was formalized: the unit was restructured and renamed the **Data Science Center (DSC)**,
with a new visual identity and a mission written to cover any discipline —

> to foster a welcoming research community by developing data literacy and foundational coding
> skills through consulting and education … supporting researchers throughout the full data life
> cycle: planning and data management plans; acquisition, storage, cleaning and usage; analysis;
> publication; curation; and preservation [@dennisEtal2021].

SSDA became a named component of it. Per Tim, Todd Grappone — then the Library's AUL for Digital
Initiatives and IT — shepherded the 2014 transfer, coined the "Data Science Center" name, and
helped design the 2018 service model.[^grappone]

[^tim-hire]: Tim Dennis, personal account, 2026-08-09.

[^grappone]: Tim Dennis, personal account. Grappone's role in the 2014 transfer and the 2018
naming is not documented in public sources; it rests on the author's account as a participant.
Grappone became University Librarian at UC Santa Barbara in July 2025.

## 2018-present: The Data Science Center

This is the era with the widest gap between the unit's size and its reach, and the era this
history's author directed — so it is documented against institutional records and cited sources,
not recollection, and the judgments in it are marked as judgments. Working notes and the full
evidence trail are in `evidence/library-era-2014-present.md` and
[history-companion.qmd](history-companion.html).

### Continuity, not rupture

The 2018 rebrand changed the unit's name and broadened its scope; it didn't replace what came
before. `ucla-data-archive_old`, a repository built around the "Data Archive" identity — its
collections policies, terms, deposit and preservation practices — was created July 2017 and
actively maintained through May 2020, two years past the point the org's formal name became
"Data Science Center." The archive's core function — repository hosting, the direct descendant of
the LAMAS/SCSS/LACSS lineage — ran underneath the new name the whole time. **Jina "Jamie"
Jamison**, who transferred with the archive in 2014, still leads on that repository work today;
she is the single human through-line across the entire Library era.

Growth over the same span is easy to state and hard to overstate. Staff went from **2.0 FTE at
the 2014 transfer** (a director and a data archivist) to **five** by roughly 2021 — most of it
by redesigning existing library positions rather than net-new hiring: a geospatial librarian
moved in from another department and rebuilt as a Spatial Data Science Librarian (Zhiyuan Yao),
a data manager from the Library's IT division rebuilt as a Data Science Facilitator, and a
Digital Library programmer with a machine-learning background recruited across divisions
(Kristian Allen, a 0.5-FTE role, 2018–2024).[^staff-model] UCLA Dataverse went from **9 datasets
and 229 downloads in January 2020** to roughly **1,600 datasets and over 143,000 downloads** by
2026 [^dataverse-count]. That growth was not matched by proportional staffing; part of how the
unit absorbed it is the student program described below, and part is that some capacity was
simply lost — a GIS position eliminated in 2024, other roles ended, with demand in those areas
undiminished.

[^staff-model]: Dennis et al. 2021 [@dennisEtal2021] describes the redesign-not-hire staffing
model. The specific position histories rest partly on the author's account. [NEEDS TIM: the
Data Science Facilitator's name and dates; Leigh Phan's exact title and start; the 5-FTE peak
year and the headcount at dissolution.]

[^dataverse-count]: The "~1,600" resolves an apparent discrepancy: UCLA Dataverse holds ~376
datasets deposited directly at UCLA plus ~1,014 legacy Social Science Data Archive datasets
harvested in and curated by Library staff (~1,390 released), and 1,603 counting drafts and
restricted deposits. UCLA's live-dashboard figure of ~377 is the directly-deposited slice. See
`evidence/library-era-2014-present.md` §4.

### What stayed constant, and what changed

Across five institutional homes and 60-plus years, the constant has been a responsibility to
make research evidence findable, usable, and preserved — extended, era by era, to whatever kind
of evidence researchers were producing. What changed after 2018 is the *range* of objects that
responsibility covers: not just survey datasets, but restricted and sensitive data requiring
governed computation, geospatial data and aerial imagery, 3D and spatial capture, text corpora
and computational text analysis, research software, and curriculum treated as a citable
output.[^text] Described after the fact, that range
tracks the field's own sequence — data citation, then open and FAIR data, then open science,
then software curation, then computationally-intensive research support — but that is a way of
narrating what changed, not a plan any year was executing. The sections below take the main
strands in turn.

[^text]: The text-analysis strand is the least documented. The DSC team's 2021 chapter
[@dennisEtal2021] cites one worked example — a consultation helping a graduate student analyze
ancient Buddhist texts with natural-language-processing techniques — and the "corpuses"
purchased with archive funds are referenced elsewhere without detail. [NEEDS TIM: the OCR /
manuscript / historical-statistical-series work and the purchased text corpora.]

### The repository: UCLA Dataverse

The legacy SSDA collection had lived on Harvard's hosted Dataverse. In 2018 the DSC stood up a
**local UCLA instance**, chosen for the same reasons the archive chose Dataverse originally —
DDI metadata, license restriction, tiered curation from self-service deposit to fully mediated —
and integrated it with UCLA single sign-on, DOI minting, and preservation alignment through the
California Digital Library. Research groups sponsor their own branded sub-collections within it,
self-administered with DSC training. A deliberate director-level choice was to **harvest** the
legacy SSDA collection into the discovery layer rather than migrate it immediately: continuity
first, migration later.

The collections DSC hosts now run well past social science: the **UCLA Law Behind Bars Data
Project** (COVID-19 in prisons, jails, and detention nationally; ~1,169 items), the **Williams
Institute** (whose LGBT law-and-policy data DSC curation helped bring to ICPSR directly —
TransPop, the first national probability sample of transgender people in the US, among them),
and the **Cotsen Institute / DIG** archaeology collections (~6,360 items in DIG alone, larger
than the entire historical SSDA/LAMAS/SCSS/LACSS corpus). DIG's own stated aim — "expand citation
practices" in archaeology — is the archive's 1980s bibliographic-control instinct, in a
different field, at a much larger scale.

Repository work also meant defending it: in early 2025, AI-driven bots mass-downloaded UCLA
Dataverse content for apparent model training, rotating across thousands of addresses to evade
blocking; DSC diagnosed the pattern and deployed an open-source filter that contained it by
mid-year.[^bots]

[^bots]: Tim Dennis, self-reported (Statement of Professional Achievements, 2023–2025). The
tool deployed was Anubis. [NEEDS TIM: a ticket or postmortem reference to anchor the dates.]

### Governed computation: Redivis and the L2 voter file

Before this, UCLA had no compliant environment for restricted, multi-terabyte national datasets
of this class — no governed way to give a student voter-file access, no secure environment for
merging FERPA/PII/PHI-restricted data at scale. To support that class of data, **DSC selected
and licensed Redivis, coordinated the institutional compliance review (Third-Party Risk
Management, P3/P4 approval), negotiated restricted-dataset access, piloted the platform in 2022,
and launched the governed service in January 2023** — a 50-seat, data-use-agreement-controlled
model so routine requests wouldn't bottleneck on one person.[^redivis-source]

The flagship case is the **L2 historic voter file** — over 10 TB of national voter history,
purchased through the archive's gift fund, that arrived as thousands of fragmented state-level
files too large to store locally and too inconsistent to analyze. DSC consolidated it into a
single version-controlled national dataset, published with its own DOI (UCLA Library, *L2 Voter
History and Demographic Dataset*, 2023, doi:10.60603/D33W2T) and presented at FORCE11 2024 by
Redivis's CEO alongside the doctoral student who curated it, Graham Straus: *"What happens when I
leave UCLA? Will people know how the dataset was constructed? Yes!"* Researchers use it directly
across departments — election administration, gentrification, Latino voting, and a project
merging the voter file with UCLA medical records to study health and voting. Recorded processing
on the platform grew from 444 GB in its first year to 2.9 PB in 2024; those figures measure
platform activity, not data held (holdings are ~20 TB). DSC provided the environment and the
access; the scholarship stayed with the researchers. The significance isn't an "AI" story — it's
the point stewardship came to include *governed computation*, not just acquiring and describing
open files.

[^redivis-source]: Platform and governance detail: Tim Dennis, Statement of Professional
Achievements and Data Summary, 2023–2025, self-reported. The DOI, the FORCE11 presentation
(Mathews & Straus 2024, doi:10.5281/zenodo.13181256), and the publication venues are the
independently checkable parts. Launch: piloted 2022, governed service launched January 2023
(confirmed by Tim 2026-09-02; reconciles the July-2022 / January-2023 sources).

### Teaching at scale, and open science

Facing tens of thousands of potential learners with a staff of two, the unit joined **The
Carpentries** in 2017 and used it to grow an instructor community rather than hire one. Tim
founded **UCLA Carpentries** in 2018 and co-founded the systemwide **UC Carpentries** network in
2020, when COVID made coordinated cross-campus training necessary; by the 2023–2025 period that
network ran 37 workshops across six campuses. As chair of Library Carpentry's Curriculum
Advisory Committee (since 2022), Tim moved several lessons into the official worldwide
curriculum, including a Data Management Plans lesson aligned to the NIH data-sharing policy.

The IMLS grant **RE-252335-OLS-22** ($237,839, Tim as Project Director) [@imls-re252335] treated
curriculum itself as a citable research output: 15 peer-reviewed open-science lessons against 14
proposed, each with a Zenodo DOI, CRediT contributor roles, ORCID identifiers, and Citation File
Format metadata, built by 27 authors across 14 teams. It is the era's clearest instance of the
"software curation" and "open science" strands, and — because a federal award is verifiable
independent of anyone's account of it — the one with the firmest external evidence.

Separately, Tim is **Co-PI on the $1.85M Sloan Foundation grant that established the UC OSPO
Network**, a six-campus effort to treat open-source software as legitimate scholarly
infrastructure. That grant funds the network, not DSC; what DSC drew from it is a **local UCLA
open-source program office**, leadership of the network's education work, and shared services
(licensing guidance, a repository browser, a summer student research program). The need is
concrete: a 2025 scan of ~81,000 UC-affiliated code repositories found 77.5% carried no license
at all.

### Spatial data, 3D capture, and the Lux Lab

Geography has consistently been the unit's single largest workshop audience. Before its GIS
position was eliminated in 2024, DSC's geospatial librarian handled 70–80 booked consultations a
year, established a systemwide **UC GIS Week**, ran UC GIS workshops that reached hundreds of
participants, managed the **LARIAC** regional aerial-imagery holdings (bought through the
archive's gift fund), and worked with UC San Diego and UC Santa Barbara on geospatial discovery
for Dataverse. DSC also ran UCLA's campus **ArcGIS Online** platform — grown to over 7,000
accounts and 3,000-plus active users a year, and, since the position was cut, running past its
licensed storage with no designated administrator.[^gis]

The clearest single case of the stewardship mission reaching a genuinely new object of research
is **Doug Daniels** and the **Lux Lab**. Daniels joined the Library in 2013 and the DSC team in
2020 as Emerging Technologies Librarian; he runs UCLA's point-cloud visualization service
(pointcloud.ucla.edu, on Potree), is FAA-certified for drone work, and has built a body of
3D-capture projects across archaeology, medicine, and cultural heritage — Easter Island Moai
models feeding a Cotsen Institute atlas, cadaver-arm scans now taught in History of Medicine, a
3D-printed surgical guide in use at the medical center, drone-LiDAR surveys in Cambodia and
Iceland, and — with DataSquad students and the Vietnamese Heritage Museum — a public 3D
narrative of a refugee family's maritime escape. He was named a UCLA Librarian of the Year for
2026. His work also runs straight back to the donor relationship: he scanned Powell Library
itself, and demonstrated the lab's work to the Powell Society donor circle.

[^gis]: GIS consultation counts and the ArcGIS figures: DSC statistics and Tim Dennis's Data
Summary, 2023–2025, cross-checked against an OARC governance report (Dec 2025) for the account
totals. [NEEDS TIM: when and from whom DSC took over ArcGIS Online administration; LARIAC
vintages and who serves that data now; and the OCR / text-corpus / digitized-document work,
which is barely documented in what's been gathered.]

### DataSquad: a student research workforce

Modeled on Carleton College's program, **DataSquad** began in 2020 on a Powell gift that funded
the first cohort's salaries and laptops, with the Library adding funds in 2023 to expand it. It
pairs undergraduate and graduate consultants with staff on sustained project work; reportable
project engagements grew from a handful in 2023 to over a hundred in 2025, as departments began
planning research around its availability rather than calling it only when something broke. Of
the ten students whose post-graduation outcomes were tracked in the 2023–2025 period, all went
into data or technical roles — McKinsey, Amazon, AIG, Stanford, CVS Health among them — and the
model has been picked up elsewhere through a DataSquad International network. Its research
contributions are documented in the spotlights under [Research impact](#research-impact).

### People and funding

Much of this era's expansion ran on **Norman Powell**'s philanthropy — a data-scientist
position, a deep-learning machine and DSC space in the Young Research Library, and DataSquad's
seed funding (all separate from his dated $5M December 2016 gift endowing the University
Librarian position). Just as important was a quieter piece of fiscal stewardship: DSC moved the
archive's large recurring subscriptions (ICPSR, Roper) off its own gift fund and onto the
Library's general membership budget — the way research libraries treat major database
memberships — which freed the archive's original fund to cover the cloud-infrastructure costs of
Dataverse and the point-cloud platform. That reallocation depended on one role having visibility
across both the archive's budget and the infrastructure budget at once.[^funding]

The people who carried the work: Jamie Jamison (repository and curation), Doug Daniels (3D and
emerging technology), Leigh Phan (programmer to data scientist over this period), a GIS/spatial
librarian, a data-science facilitator, and the rotating DataSquad students. The full roster,
with what is and isn't independently documented, is in
[history-companion.qmd](history-companion.html).

[^funding]: The subscription-to-general-fund move and the reinvestment into infrastructure are
confirmed in direction by budget ledgers and AWS cost records; the full dollar trail (and the
dates two other subscriptions were dropped) is partly reconstructed. See
`evidence/library-era-2014-present.md` §13. [NEEDS TIM: the budget records for the
infrastructure and dataset purchases funded from the freed line.]

## Research impact

Two different things get measured here, and they answer different questions.

### Historical traces of reuse

**Holdings activity** shows when the archive's deposited datasets were originally collected, by
decade — a proxy for how active the archive itself was. **Citation evidence** shows which of
that data is documented as having been used in later published research — a proxy for downstream
value, not for the archive's own activity. They don't share an axis, and shouldn't be read
against each other directly: a decade with heavy collecting activity doesn't necessarily produce
more citations, and citations can (and here, do) arrive decades after collection.

### Contemporary research enabled

The 2018-present section above covers the infrastructure — Dataverse, Redivis, the Carpentries
and open-science work, the spatial and 3D services — and the funding behind it. What that
infrastructure carried, with the independently checkable part called out:

| Case | What's independently checkable |
|---|---|
| Redivis / L2 restricted data | Publication venues (APSR, PNAS, BJPolS, AEJ), a public dataset DOI, a public FORCE11 presentation |
| IMLS open-science grant | A federal grant award record, public lesson repositories, Library Carpentry's own adoption record |
| Carceral Ecologies (Nicholas Shapiro) | DSC/DataSquad multi-year support on a helicopter-surveillance dataset; national media (*LA Times*, *The New Yorker*, *Bloomberg*); pilot data behind the $5.07M Dana Foundation grant (2023) that established the UCLA–Charles R. Drew Dana Center for Neuroscience & Society, where Shapiro is Director of Research |
| BioCritical Studies Lab (Terence Keel) | Multi-year DataSquad work on a US deaths-in-custody dataset; a 2024 UCLA Public Impact Research Award; DSC's work credited in Keel's book *The Coroner's Silence* |
| Refugee Material Culture Initiative (Kelly Nguyen) | Doug Daniels + DataSquad, with the Vietnamese Heritage Museum; a public 3D digital narrative |
| DataSquad | Student outcomes for the ten tracked graduates (data/technical roles); the projects above drew independent national coverage |

## Methods and limitations

The author's position is stated up front, in "A note on the author's position." Tim Dennis
directed the unit for the recent decades this history covers, and is separately the author of
documents (a grant proposal, reorg-response material) that draw on some of the same facts for
advocacy. A repository boundary doesn't change that. What this project does instead:

- The author's role, and this project's relationship to `ospo_datasquad_grant`, are stated
  plainly rather than left for the reader to discover.
- Facts are sourced to a claim register (`dsc-evidence-registry`), not asserted from memory —
  see `claims/ssda-*`, `claims/icpsr-*`, `claims/issr-*`, `claims/dennis-*`, `claims/dsc-*` there
  for what's verified vs. disputed vs. self-reported.
- Documented facts are kept separate from institutional interpretation; discontinuities, gaps,
  and contested points are stated as such, not smoothed over — see README.md "Known gaps" and
  [history-companion.qmd](history-companion.html) "Open discrepancies."
- `ospo_datasquad_grant` may cite this project's evidence, but it is not independent
  corroboration of a claim that traces back to the same author.
- **Self-reported achievement claims** (much of the 2018-present detail comes from Tim's and
  Doug's own internal personnel-review documents) are treated as discovery sources, not sole
  public evidence. Where independent corroboration exists (press coverage, award records,
  publication venues, grant award pages), the claim is included and the corroboration is what's
  cited. Where only the review document supports a claim, it's either omitted or explicitly
  attributed as a self-reported account — see [history-companion.qmd](history-companion.html)
  for what's been held to that standard.
- The evidence cutoff is 2026-08-31. An outside read for factual support and proportion is
  optional, at the author's discretion; if one happens, the reader is named in "A note on the
  author's position."
